body.objective: Students will be able to draw with contour and gesture.
body.iCan: I can draw with contour and gesture.
successCriteria: I can draw quick gesture drawings that capture movement
I can draw slow contour lines from observation
I can explain how each method helps me see
body.hook: Most people draw what they think something looks like, not what they actually see. A gesture drawing takes 30 seconds and captures energy; a contour drawing takes 10 minutes and captures every edge. Together they train your eye to see like an artist.

vocabulary.definition: A quick, loose drawing that captures the movement and energy of a subject.
A line that follows the edges and surface changes of a form.
Drawing a contour without looking at the paper.
Looking carefully at a real subject while drawing.
How a line varies in thickness, darkness and speed.
Measuring angles and proportions by eye, often with a pencil held at arm's length.

study.title: Seeing Like an Artist
study.question: How do gesture and contour drawing help me really see?
study.passage:
Part 1, Gesture warm-up (10 minutes): A classmate holds short poses (30 seconds, then 1 minute, then 2 minutes). Draw the whole figure with loose, continuous lines. Start with the line of action, a curve showing the main direction of the pose.
Part 2, Blind contour (10 minutes): Draw your non-drawing hand or a shoe without looking at the paper. Move your eyes and pencil slowly at the same speed along every edge. The result will look strange; that's the point. You're training your eye, not making a finished drawing.
Part 3, Modified contour (20 minutes): Draw a still life (a backpack, a plant, a crumpled bag). Look at the paper only to place your pencil. Vary line quality: press harder for edges closer to you or in shadow, lighter for distant or lit edges.
Part 4, Sighting: hold your pencil at arm's length, close one eye, and compare the height and width of the object before drawing.
Reflection: Compare your first and last drawings. What do you notice now that you missed before?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Draw a modified contour of a still life
Reflect on what you now notice
discussion: What did gesture drawing help you capture that contour drawing didn't?
Why does blind contour feel uncomfortable, and why is it useful?
How did varying line quality change your still life?
How did sighting change your proportions?
study.product: Complete a page of five gesture drawings and one finished modified contour drawing with varied line quality, and write a paragraph on how your observation changed.

examples.title: Gesture
examples.problem: What should you draw first in a gesture?
steps: The main direction of the pose

examples.title: Line quality
examples.answer: Heavier lines for near or shadowed edges, lighter for far edges
examples.explore: Where would you use your darkest line?

examples.title: Blind contour
examples.problem: Why not look at the paper?
steps: Forces your eye to follow the subject
examples.answer: It trains you to draw what you see, not what you expect

examples.title: Sighting
examples.problem: How do you compare height and width?
examples.answer: Measure the height on the pencil, then turn it to compare the width
